query: For a CoCrFeNi high-entropy-alloy matrix evaluated in sliding from room temperature to 800 °C, what single intervention could overcome the difficulty of maintaining low coefficient of friction and wear rate throughout the full temperature range? Formulate one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains the mechanism expected to operate across the test regime, predicts performance relative to the starting CoCrFeNi material, specifies relevant temperature, load, and environmental boundaries, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes a controlled falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: Doping the CoCrFeNi high‐entropy alloy with an optimum amount of Nb (e.g., around 5 wt%) will generate a dual‐phase microstructure (FCC plus a hard Laves phase) that promotes the in situ formation of a protective, potentially lubricious oxide/tribolayer at the sliding interface. This microstructural and surface‐chemical evolution is expected to yield a consistently low coefficient of friction and reduced wear rate across the full temperature range from room temperature to 800 °C compared to the undoped alloy.
generation.material_initial_state: Undoped CoCrFeNi high‐entropy alloy with a single-phase FCC structure.
generation.intervention: Introduce Nb doping (approximately 5 wt%) during alloy synthesis.
generation.conditions: Sliding wear tests conducted in ambient atmosphere over a temperature range from room temperature (~25 °C) to 800 °C, under representative high contact pressures and loads typical for tribological evaluation.
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of a dual-phase microstructure, with the Nb addition inducing a Laves phase alongside the FCC matrix; plus, at elevated temperatures, Nb is expected to form stable oxides that act as self-lubricating tribolayers.
generation.mechanism: Nb addition induces lattice distortion and phase transformation that increases hardness and facilitates the formation of finely dispersed Laves phase particles. Under sliding, these microstructural features help resist wear, while the Nb-enriched regions oxidize at high temperatures to generate a protective lubricious oxide layer. Together, these factors reduce friction and wear consistently across a wide temperature range.
generation.predicted_outcome: The Nb-doped CoCrFeNi HEA is expected to exhibit a lower coefficient of friction and reduced wear rate over the full 25 °C to 800 °C range compared to the baseline undoped alloy.
generation.baseline: CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy without Nb addition, which shows increased wear and a higher friction coefficient at elevated temperatures.
generation.boundary: This improvement is anticipated under sliding conditions (e.g., ball-on-disk tests) with high contact pressures in ambient air, from room temperature up to 800 °C; the interplay of ductile and hard phases must be maintained without excessive brittleness.
generation.uncertainty: The exact magnitude of friction reduction and wear improvement, as well as the stability and lubricity of the Nb-derived oxide layer at the highest temperatures, remains to be quantitatively determined. Potential trade-offs between enhanced hardness and possible brittleness at elevated Nb contents need further evaluation.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of CoCrFeNi samples: one set doped with approximately 5 wt% Nb and one undoped (control). Perform systematic ball-on-disk sliding wear tests under identical conditions, across a temperature range from room temperature to 800 °C. Characterize microstructure before and after tests using SEM/EDS and XRD, and evaluate tribofilms by XPS or Raman spectroscopy.
measurements: Coefficient of friction as a function of temperature
Wear rate (mm³/(N∙m)) at each temperature step
Phase composition and surface chemistry of the worn regions
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Nb-doped samples do not show a statistically significant (e.g., >15% improvement) reduction in friction coefficient and wear rate across all tested temperatures compared to the undoped alloy, or if the expected dual-phase microstructure and protective oxide/tribolayer are not observed in post-test analyses, then the hypothesis is falsified.

## Abstract
A series of five-element CoCrFeNi-Nbx (x = 0, 1, 3, 5, 7, and 9 wt%) high-entropy alloys were prepared using high-energy ball milling and discharge plasma sintering methods. Then, the effects of doping with Nb elements on the organization and properties of the CoCrFeNi HEAs were systematically investigated by tensile testing, hardness testing, and examining their micro-morphologies. The results show that with the addition of the Nb element, the lattice distortion of the alloy due to the large size of the Nb atoms causes the microstructure of CoCrFeNi HEAs to change from a single-phase FCC structure to a dual-phase structure of FCC and Laves. With the increase in the Nb content, the increase in the volume fraction of the hard and brittle Laves phase leads to the enhancement of the HEA’s tensile strength, yield strength, and hardness, and a decrease in plasticity. The Nb5 alloy showed the most excellent comprehensive performance, with a tensile strength, yield strength, and plasticity of 879.1 MPa, 491.8 MPa, and 39.8%, respectively, and all the properties were improved compared with those of the HEAs obtained by the arc melting method. AbstractQ235B is widely used in marine engineering materials; however, its wear resistance and corrosion resistance are poor. To improve wear and corrosion resistance, a CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy (HEA) composite coating was cladded using laser cladding (LC) technology. Different proportions of tungsten carbide (WC) and Nb elements were added to the CoCrFeNi HEA coating, and the microstructure, phase, hardness, wear, and corrosion resistance of three different composite coatings were analyzed. The results show that the in situ synthetic phase is composed of Face central cubic (FCC) (Cr3C2) and strengthening phases such as W, WC, and NbC. In the process of LC, Nb will react with WC in situ, which not only reduces the morphology of the CoCrFeNi HEA cladding coating changed by adding WC, but also generates NbC, which leads to the dissolution of WC particles and improves the uniformity of particle distribution of the coating. The hardness of the coating with Nb is increased by 1.40 times, the wear resistance is enhanced, and the peeling of the hard phase is reduced during wear.
